kesavananda_bharati_1973.reference_summary: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru and Ors. v. State of Kerala and Anr. was a constitutional case concerning the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368. The petitioner challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act and, during the proceedings, also challenged the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, and the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972. The central issues included whether Parliament's amending power was unlimited, whether Constitutional amendments were subject to Article 13(2), and whether Parliament could alter or destroy the basic structure of the Constitution. The Court held that Constitutional amendments made under Article 368 were not ordinary laws within Article 13(2), but Parliament's amending power was subject to limitations arising from the basic structure of the Constitution. The Twenty-fourth Amendment was upheld. Section 2 of the Twenty-fifth Amendment was upheld, while the part of Section 3 that excluded judicial review through a declaration was held invalid. The Twenty-ninth Amendment was upheld. The judgment established the Basic Structure Doctrine, under which Parliament cannot alter or destroy the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution.
